intros.market: Five CAs control 88.78% of global issuance, led by Internet Security Research Group at 32.6% and Google Trust Services at 21.0%. The market concentration ratio (CR3 = 71.41%, HHI = 2015) indicates moderate concentration, though 74 tail CAs collectively account for the remaining ~11% of issuance. This distribution creates a two-tier ecosystem where a handful of high-volume providers serve most websites while dozens of smaller CAs maintain full trust store inclusion despite minimal market presence.
intros.trust: 335 roots are distributed across four trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores and just 38 CA owners achieve universal trust. Microsoft's store contains 142 roots not trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating significant operational complexity for certificate chain validation. These disagreements mean a certificate chain valid in Edge may fail in Chrome or Safari, forcing CAs to maintain multiple hierarchies and website operators to test across browser environments.
intros.conc: The top three CAs account for 71.41% of all issuance (HHI = 2015), creating systemic dependency on Internet Security Research Group, Google Trust Services, and DigiCert. A technical or compliance failure at any of these providers would immediately affect hundreds of millions of websites. This concentration has grown alongside declining root program oversight, with governance coverage rates falling from 67-78% in 2019 to under 20% in 2025.
intros.tail: 74 CAs operate with minimal issuance volume yet maintain full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk exposure for browsers and users. These tail CAs collectively represent just 11% of issuance but account for a disproportionate share of governance and operational incidents. Low transaction volume means less operational maturity and fewer resources for compliance infrastructure, yet their roots carry the same browser trust as high-volume providers.
intros.geo: CAs incorporated in the United States account for 92.75% of global issuance across 15 organizations, while 44 European CAs collectively issue just 7.16% and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs contribute 0.09%. This geographic concentration mirrors market concentration, with US-based Internet Security Research Group, Google Trust Services, and DigiCert dominating global supply. Europe maintains the most CA organizations but minimal issuance share, while Asia-Pacific and other regions operate primarily for domestic or niche markets.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs maintain trust store presence but account for only 0.09% of global issuance. These entities pose unique risks because they operate under state authority and may face compelled disclosure or surveillance requirements that differ from commercial CAs. Most government CAs serve domestic constituencies in Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East/Africa regions, appearing in the long tail of low-volume issuers.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk for compelled disclosure and state surveillance: China, Russia, United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk under current legal frameworks. These classifications reflect national security laws that may compel CAs to produce private keys, issue certificates under government direction, or provide access to validation records, creating potential for man-in-the-middle attacks against encrypted connections.
intros.ops: 1,674 incidents have been filed across 55 CAs, dominated by misissuance (645), governance failures (539), and revocation issues (360). Only 29% of incidents are discovered by the CA itself, while 18% are found by external researchers and 16% by automated tools, revealing a significant self-surveillance gap. Root program oversight directly identifies just 4% of incidents, with audit findings contributing 8%, leaving most problems to be surfaced by external parties rather than internal controls or formal audits.
intros.crypto: The cryptographic posture tab examines root certificate algorithms, key sizes, and compliance with current standards across all 335 trusted roots. RSA 2048-bit keys remain the dominant standard, with gradual migration toward 4096-bit keys and elliptic curve alternatives. Post-quantum readiness remains minimal across the ecosystem, with no production deployments yet visible in trusted root infrastructure despite NIST's published PQC standards.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have occurred across the ecosystem, with 14 attributed to compliance or operational failures and 10 following a pattern of repeated issues. Seven cases involved negligent noncompliance, three demonstrated incompetence, and three showed willful circumvention of requirements. The median runway from distrust announcement to root removal is 1,185 days (3.2 years), giving affected CAs substantial time to transition customers but extending the window during which compromised infrastructure remains trusted.
intros.policy: 43 active TLS issuers face three compliance milestones for certificate validity reduction under SC-081: 200 days (March 2026), 100 days (March 2027), and 47 days (March 2029). Measured by actual replacement behavior, 3 CAs remain at risk for the 200-day threshold, 5 for the 100-day threshold, with a median current validity of 63 days. This readiness challenge occurs against a regulatory surface that has grown 121x since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations (76% mandatory) across CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root programs, WebTrust/ETSI audit criteria, and IETF/ISO/NIST standards, with complexity increasing faster than operational maturity.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 67.8% (Chrome) and 78.0% (Mozilla) in 2019 to 18.4% and 9.9% respectively in 2025, with Apple at 5.4% and Microsoft providing no substantive oversight. Chrome has participated in 732 oversight bugs with 293 substantive interventions (112 recent), while Mozilla shows 819 oversight bugs but declining recent engagement (47 substantive). This withdrawal occurs as incident volumes remain high and the long tail of 74 low-volume CAs continues operating with minimal scrutiny, creating a governance vacuum at the infrastructure layer of internet encryption.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership but only 21 contribute actively, with 35 maintaining zero participation. Sectigo leads organizational contribution, while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1. This silent majority pattern means a small group of active participants shapes policy for an ecosystem serving billions of users, with most CAs consuming rather than contributing to governance development.
intros.audit: Auditors caught just 28% of incidents that occurred during the audit period they reviewed, meaning 118 of 429 in-scope incidents appeared in audit letters while 311 went undetected. 42 CAs show high transparency gaps between clean audit opinions and documented incident histories, with 5 qualified opinions issued and 8 auditor changes in 2025. WebTrust CAs self-report 62.5% of their audit letters while ETSI CAs self-report 68.7%, leaving significant gaps in audit repository completeness. This surveillance failure connects directly to the operational risk finding that CAs discover only 29% of their own incidents, revealing systemic weakness in both internal controls and external audit effectiveness.
